Suppressions & Holds

Protection-order suppressions block reads at ingest. Evidence holds preserve records past retention. Releasing either takes two keys — two different authorized operators, in sequence.

🔑 Answer key — how to clear the fence & complete a release

Fence F-07 standing · start at step 1

You've seen the locked door — a release that takes both keys and still won't go through. This is the key. Follow these four steps in order; each one ticks off here as you do it, and each one writes its own entry to the Audit Log so you can watch the record build.

  1. 1
    Open divergence D-118 and look at what actually disagrees.
    The fence is standing because two checkpoints disagree. Nothing can be released until a person has seen that disagreement — not just that it exists.
  2. 2
    Accept the divergence — as a second supervisor.
    In the review, pick Lt. A. Osei (acceptance can't come from the operator the fence is holding — it has to be a second pair of eyes), tick the attestation, and accept. Escalating instead is also a valid answer: it keeps the fence up and hands D-118 upward, and that choice is logged too.
  3. 3
    The fence clears.
    On acceptance, fence F-07 comes down everywhere at once — header pill, Audit Log and System Health all flip to cleared, and ceremony / release endpoints unfence. No separate “clear fence” button exists on purpose: accepting the divergence is the key turn.
  4. 4
    Now release something — two different keys + a reason.
    Use any Release… button below (try suppression href:41be…07c2, Order 2026-DR-221). Key 1 and Key 2 must be different operators, and a reason is required. This time it completes, the item shows Released, and the completed release appears at the top of the Audit Log.

Stuck? If you try step 4 before steps 1–3, you'll get the blocked message again — that's deliberate, and even that blocked attempt is logged (see “What gets logged” below).

What gets logged for a release — yes, logging is mandatory

Audit chain · append-only

There is no silent release in NOCTUA. Every release action writes to the hash-chained audit log — the blocked attempts as well as the completed ones. You can't turn a key “off the record”: the log entry is created by the same action that turns the key, not as a separate step an operator could forget.

Written to the chain, every time
  • Who — both key-turners, by name (Key 1 and Key 2 are recorded separately, in order)
  • What — the kind of release (suppression or evidence hold) and its ID — e.g. hold EH-2026-031
  • When — timestamp in Central Time
  • Why — the release reason, recorded as entered (that's why the form won't submit without one)
  • Fence state at that moment — standing or cleared, and the divergence ID (D-118) and how it was decided
  • Outcome — completed, or BLOCKED — fence standing. A blocked attempt is a permanent entry, not an error that vanishes
  • Chain link — each entry stores the previous entry's hash and gets its own (prev → hash), so a later edit breaks every entry after it
Never written to the log
  • The raw plate of a suppressed vehicle. Suppressions are referenced only by their keyed reference — href:41be…07c2 — in the release entry, the blocked-read entries, everywhere. The plate itself never enters the chain.
  • Anything about the protected person behind an order — the log names the order (2026-DR-221), never the person it protects.
Try it and watch it happen
  • Accept D-118 above, complete a release, then open Audit Log: your acceptance, the fence clearing, and the completed release are the newest entries at the top, each linked prev → hash.

What happens on confirm: Units are dispatched, the hit clears from the queue, and the disposition is written to the audit chain. Cancelling leaves the hit untouched in the queue.

Two-key release

Releasing requires two different authorized operators, in sequence. Both turns are written to the audit chain.

Fence check: divergence D-118 is unaccepted. This release will be recorded as attempted under a standing fence and cannot complete until the divergence is accepted or escalated.

Logging: turning these keys writes to the audit chain either way — both operators, this item, the time, your reason, the fence state, and the outcome (completed, or BLOCKED). For a suppression, the entry carries the keyed reference (href:…) only — never the raw plate. See “What gets logged for a release” on this page for the full list.

Divergence D-118 — review & decide

This is the disagreement the fence is standing on. Acceptance is an informed act: read both checkpoints below first — they are what you are being asked to accept.

Why is there a fence at all? Fence F-07 was raised on a file-state record, then promoted to a divergence at 22:30 CT when a checkpoint disagreed with it. While any divergence is unaccepted, the fence stands and no release can complete — so that nobody releases a hold or suppression while the system's own record-keeping is in question.

What actually disagrees: one field only — the anchor set. The reported checkpoint says the promoted record belongs to anchor set B; the fence record on file still calls it set A. Entry counts match, there are no breaks, and no entries are missing on either side. Accepting D-118 means: the record is corrected to anchor set B, and the fence comes down. If that correction doesn't look right to you, escalate instead — the fence stays up and D-118 goes to the next level with your name on the escalation.

Must be a second supervisor — not Sgt. Keller, the operator the fence is holding. Acceptance by the held operator is refused and logged as refused.

Logging: whichever you choose — accept or escalate — is written to the audit chain immediately, with your name, the time, D-118, and the exact checkpoint values shown above.
